Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space

Yanke Song    Shuo Chen    Chris Rockwell    Guande He    Nan Liu    Desai Xie    Tianpei Gu    Yong-Hyun Park    Aryan V S    Dennis Yuren Menn Affiliation: Roblox  University of California, Merced  University of Pennsylvania  University of Texas at Austin    Ming-Hsuan Yang    Xun Huang
Abstract

Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation – doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within ∼1.3\sim 1.3M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at 2×2\times higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

1 Introduction

Early video diffusion models [32, 30] generated videos in their native form, as sequences of pixel frames. As models scaled up, the field made two shifts away from pixel space: The first followed latent diffusion [72], moving generation into the latent space of a pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE) [48], initially with one latent per frame [7, 6]. The second extended the compression to time, using 3D VAEs to merge every few frames into a single latent that corresponds to no individual frame [93, 85]. For generating short clips offline at moderate resolution, this was a favorable trade: compression made training tractable at scale, at the cost of a frozen VAE that ruled out end-to-end training and capped quality at its reconstruction [14, 23, 77].

Video generation models have since outgrown this setting: they now power real-time interactive world models [27, 79, 33] through causal few-step distillation [97, 38], and serve as geometry-conditioned renderers for editing and games [43, 62, 63]. Yet these systems inherit the VAE’s fixed compression in space and time, which works against each new demand. Under a real-time compute budget, doubling the resolution yields 4×4\times more tokens and 16×16\times more attention compute, while cutting tokens requires a more aggressive VAE that further reduces quality. Precise editing requires conditions aligned to individual frames, but when several frames share one latent, fast motion blurs and objects deform (Fig. 5). Temporal compression also limits responsiveness. Since common latent world models [97, 38, 92, 27, 79, 37] autoregressively generate frames in blocks, the frame corresponding to a control cannot be generated until all controls for the full block are received. This results in a minimum control-to-screen latency proportional to the block size, a barrier that no model-side optimization can remove.

These limitations motivate removing the VAE altogether and generating every frame directly as pixels, which naively would bring back the token counts and training costs that latent models avoid. Recent pixel-space image models overcome both challenges [50, 98, 19, 18, 41, 13] by modeling semantics over large pixel patches [50] and delegating fine details to a lightweight decoder [19], thus keeping the token count and training cost reasonable. Moreover, although training video models from scratch demands prohibitive data and compute resources, a pretrained latent model already captures high-level semantics and dynamics. Hence, finetuning it into a pixel space video model only requires changing the output interface, which is a more feasible task.

In this work, we present PixVid, a recipe that lifts a pretrained latent video diffusion model into a frame-wise pixel-space model, in which every token covers a 1×p×p1\times p\times p patch of exactly one frame, so no condition or action spans multiple frames. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer (DiT) and replaces both the encoder and the decoder from the VAE (Fig. 2). At input, a patch embedding that initializes from the VAE encoder allows the DiT to start training from close to its pretrained latent distribution. At output, a lightweight detailer head renders the DiT tokens into pixels; it is convolutional to suppress the patch-grid artifacts of a linear head [88], and causal in time to allow autoregressive generation. We further identify the following key techniques: 1) predicting clean video (xx-prediction) rather than velocity, since velocity prediction forces the network to model full-rank per-pixel noise [50]; 2) using a larger noise shift, since redundant pixels retain more signal at the same noise level; and 3) using the Euler sampler, since pixel color values are numerically sensitive to higher order solvers like UniPC [101].

Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B [85], PixVid converges within 1.31.3M training clips sampled from 6464K videos, or about 44K B200 GPU-hours. It achieves competitive quality with the original latent model on VBench [39], and the recipe transfers across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2-based models with different VAEs. Generating frame by frame in pixels, it introduces several benefits, as shown in Fig. 1. Resolution: doubling the patch size lets PixVid generate 960×1664960\times 1664 with the same number of tokens per frame as at 480×832480\times 832. Control: with the same control branch as the latent model, depth-conditioned editing keeps 98%98\% of the source’s fast motion, versus 83%83\% for an identically finetuned latent model. Latency: after autoregressive distillation, each camera control takes effect at the next frame rather than the next block, cutting median latency from 495495 ms to 3434 ms while still streaming in real time.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose PixVid, a recipe that lifts a pretrained latent video diffusion model into a frame-wise pixel-space model, converging quickly to competitive quality.

  • •

    We identify the design choices that make this lift work: a causal convolutional detailer head with 9×9\times fewer patch seams than a linear head, xx-prediction with 80×80\times less pixel noise than vv-prediction, and a larger noise shift than the latent model.

  • •

    We show frame-wise pixel generation overcomes three structural limitations of latent models: resolution scaling, control alignment under fast motion, and control-to-screen latency.

2 Related Work

Pixel-Space Diffusion. Latent diffusion [72, 68, 7] has been favored for efficient training using spatial and temporal compression for video [93, 85, 8], at the price of a VAE reconstruction bottleneck. Pixel-space diffusion models for images [29, 78, 22, 46] and videos [32, 30, 76, 5] bypass a VAE but become costly at high resolution, historically requiring cascaded or multi-resolution designs [31, 74, 71, 26, 20, 81]. Recent methods improved pixel-space image generation, training from scratch [34, 35, 15, 50, 98, 19, 58, 87, 55, 57, 13, 61] or finetuning from latent checkpoints to make training tenable [18, 41, 13]. Pixel-space video generation is less explored. Concurrent works train from scratch, and they either focus on smaller class-conditioned benchmarks [84] or have undesirable patch artifacts [88]. We finetune a pretrained latent video model, inheriting its prior capabilities and maintaining competitive quality.

Controllable Video Generation and Editing. Early video editors applied image diffusion models with heuristics such as cross-frame shared self-attention [89, 70, 47, 24] or propagated edits [4, 91, 67]. Video diffusion models improve consistency and robustness, with recent models producing precise, aligned edits and structure-guided generation [43, 94, 45, 62, 49, 73, 10, 25].

Interactive Video Generation. Interactive generation produces frames as a stream, typically with autoregressive video diffusion models [11, 21, 90, 80, 12]. Combined with few-step distillation [96, 95, 97, 38, 92, 104, 17], latent world models respond to user actions across diverse scenes in real time [27, 60, 79, 33], but temporal compression delays each action, e.g. by up to three frames for Wan’s four-frame latents [85]. Per-frame latent [9, 83] and pixel-space [2, 65] world models avoid this delay but are trained from scratch on a single genre. PixVid is finetuned from a general pretrained model and responds to actions at the next frame.

3 Methods

Our goal is to generate every frame directly in pixels without training a pixel-space video model from scratch, while removing the VAE bottleneck. PixVid achieves this by lifting a pretrained latent video diffusion model into a frame-wise pixel-space model, as shown in Fig. 2. We describe its architecture in Sec. 3.1 and how we train it from the latent model in Sec. 3.2, including key design choices. We then adapt it to efficient high-resolution generation in Sec. 3.3, precise video editing in Sec. 3.4, and low-latency autoregressive generation in Sec. 3.5.

3.1 Architecture

PixVid keeps the DiT [68] backbone of a pretrained latent video model and replaces the VAE: a linear patch embedding maps pixels to tokens, and a lightweight convolutional detailer head renders the DiT outputs directly into pixels.

Frame-Wise Tokenization. Latent video models merge several frames into one latent [93, 85], so conditions apply to groups of frames. PixVid instead gives each frame its own tokens, each covering a 1×p×p1\times p\times p pixel patch. Conditions then align with individual frames, and an autoregressive model can respond to actions at the next frame. Although this approach uses more tokens per clip than with temporal compression, the spatial token count does not grow with resolution as it is determined by the adjustable patch size rather than a frozen VAE.

Detailer Head. Since the DiT captures global structure and leaves only local details to render, we implement the detailer as a lightweight 3D convolutional decoder, sharing this insight with pixel-space image models [19, 18, 41]. Unlike their U-Net detailers, which also encode the noisy pixels of each patch, ours keeps only the decoder path and reads only the DiT tokens. It stacks L=log2⁡pL=\log_{2}p up blocks, each upsampling by 1×2×21\times 2\times 2, so the head maps each token to a 1×p×p1\times p\times p pixel patch and predicts the clean video. Its convolutions also run across neighboring tokens rather than within each patch, which largely suppresses checkerboard artifacts at token boundaries. They are causal in time, so the detailer models local temporal structure without reading future frames and supports frame-by-frame generation. See App. A.2 for details.

3.2 Training from a Latent Model

PixVid finetunes end-to-end in pixel space from a pretrained latent model, with initialized DiT and input patchification, 𝒙\bm{x}-prediction, a larger noise shift, and auxiliary losses.

Initialization. To retain the pretrained latent model’s prior, we inherit its DiT weights and randomly initialize the detailer head. Following AsymFlow [13], we approximate the VAE encoder with a linear map 𝑨\bm{A} fitted offline between pixel patches and their latents, and compose it with the pretrained patch embedding to initialize the pixel patch embedding. We further employ an internal timestep calibration, with scale cc estimated alongside 𝑨\bm{A}, to ensure the signal-to-noise ratios of latent and pixel spaces are aligned. The DiT thus initially receives inputs close to the latents it was trained on. Full details appear in App. A.1.

𝒙\bm{x}-Prediction. Under flow matching [53], a clean video 𝒙\bm{x} is corrupted with Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}) at noise level σ∈[0,1]\sigma\in[0,1] as 𝒙σ=(1−σ)​𝒙+σ​ϵ\bm{x}_{\sigma}=(1-\sigma)\,\bm{x}+\sigma\,\bm{\epsilon}. Following JiT [50], the network predicts the clean video 𝒙^=𝒙θ​(𝒙σ,σ)\hat{\bm{x}}=\bm{x}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{\sigma},\sigma), and we compute the flow matching loss in velocity space,

ℒflow=𝔼𝒙,ϵ,σ​‖𝒗^−𝒗‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x},\bm{\epsilon},\sigma}\big\|\hat{\bm{v}}-\bm{v}\big\|_{2}^{2}, (1)

where 𝒗^=(𝒙σ−𝒙^)/max⁡(σ,σmin)\hat{\bm{v}}=(\bm{x}_{\sigma}-\hat{\bm{x}})/\max(\sigma,\sigma_{\min}) and 𝒗=(𝒙σ−𝒙)/max⁡(σ,σmin)\bm{v}=(\bm{x}_{\sigma}-\bm{x})/\max(\sigma,\sigma_{\min}) are the predicted and target velocities, and σmin\sigma_{\min} clips the denominator to avoid numerical instability at low noise levels. Latent models typically predict 𝒗\bm{v} while pixel-space image models either predict 𝒗\bm{v} [19, 18, 98] or switch to 𝒙\bm{x} [50, 41]. We find 𝒙\bm{x}-prediction essential for video, as it enables the detailer to render the DiT tokens into clean local structure that lies near a low-dimensional manifold [50]. Predicting 𝒗\bm{v} would instead require the network to model the full-rank per-pixel noise in 𝒙σ\bm{x}_{\sigma}, a burden that increases with patch size. Figure 9 shows 𝒗\bm{v}-prediction fills the video with high-frequency, flickering noise.

Auxiliary Losses. The temporal convolutions of the detailer are trained from scratch, so we add a loss on frame differences to learn temporal smoothness,

ℒtemp=𝔼𝒙,ϵ,σ​ρ​(Δ​𝒙^−Δ​𝒙),\mathcal{L}_{\text{temp}}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x},\bm{\epsilon},\sigma}\,\rho\big(\Delta\hat{\bm{x}}-\Delta\bm{x}\big), (2)

where Δ​𝒙(f)=𝒙(f+1)−𝒙(f)\Delta\bm{x}^{(f)}=\bm{x}^{(f+1)}-\bm{x}^{(f)} is the difference between consecutive frames ff and f+1f+1, and ρ⁡(u)=u2+δ2\rho(u)=\sqrt{u^{2}+\delta^{2}} is the Charbonnier penalty with a small constant δ\delta, averaged over all elements. We also add an LPIPS perceptual loss [99] on 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}}, which improves the visual quality of pixel-space image models [59]. Both losses are weighted toward low noise levels, where 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}} is informative. The total loss is thus

ℒ=ℒflow+λtemp​ℒtemp+λLPIPS​ℒLPIPS,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}+\lambda_{\text{temp}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{temp}}+\lambda_{\text{LPIPS}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{LPIPS}}, (3)

where λtemp\lambda_{\text{temp}} and λLPIPS\lambda_{\text{LPIPS}} are loss weights.

3.3 Efficient High-Resolution Generation

The high-level semantic content of a video changes little with resolution, so higher resolution should mainly require finer rendering, not more tokens. A latent DiT cannot exploit this, as doubling the resolution yields 4×4\times more latent tokens. PixVid instead doubles the patch size from pp to 2​p2p and adds one up block to the detailer, keeping the token grid unchanged (Fig. 3). Unlike PixelDiT [98], whose token count grows with resolution, or DiP [19] and L2P [18], which add no detailer levels, this gives the doubled resolution its own upsampling level without much additional cost.

We finetune the patch-2​p2p model from the patch-pp model. Its patch embedding fuses 2×22\times 2 average pooling with the patch-pp embedding, so the DiT initially sees a downsampled version of its input, and the new upsampling block starts as an identity pass-through, acting as nearest-neighbor upsampling. We also double both the calibration scale and the noise shift [23], so the DiT sees the same noise schedule as at patch pp. See App. A.3 for details.

3.4 Precise Video Editing

Precise video editing, such as re-rendering a video from its per-frame depth, requires the generated video to align with the condition at every frame. Latent models typically encode the condition with the same VAE as the video [43], so several condition frames share one latent, leading to inaccurate alignment, especially in fast motions. In PixVid, the condition is tokenized per frame as the corresponding video, so generation and condition are aligned at the frame level, without changing the conditioning mechanism. Concretely, we add the control branch of VACE [43]: conditions are residually added to the DiT tokens via control blocks, and the condition’s patch embedding is initialized, like the video’s, by fusing the pretrained embedding with 𝑨\bm{A}.

3.5 Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation

Interactive applications stream video in response to user controls, such as camera or motion inputs, and should react to each control as soon as it arrives. An autoregressive model generates video in blocks, and a block can start only once the controls for all its frames have arrived. In a temporally compressed latent model, each block spans at least one latent, i.e., several frames, so a new control waits for the rest of its block, a delay that no throughput-side optimization can remove (Fig. 6). PixVid can generate single-frame blocks, so each control takes effect at the next frame. To achieve this, we lift a bidirectional latent model to pixel space with the recipe above and distill it into a few-step causal model with Self Forcing [38]. The causal detailer decodes one frame at a time from cached features of previous frames, keeping its cost per frame constant. Single-frame blocks trade some throughput for this latency gain, which we analyze in Sec. 4.5.

4 Experiments

We evaluate PixVid on text-to-video generation in Sec. 4.2, followed by its three applications: efficient high-resolution generation in Sec. 4.3, precise video editing in Sec. 4.4, and low-latency autoregressive generation in Sec. 4.5. Finally, we ablate our key design choices in Sec. 4.6.

4.1 Experimental Setup

We lift three pretrained latent models into pixel space: Wan2.1-T2V-14B [85] for text-to-video and high-resolution generation, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for video editing and ablations, and the camera-controlled SolarWM-5B [37] for interactive generation. Unless otherwise noted, models generate 2121-frame videos with patch size p=16p=16 and sample with 5050 Euler steps at the training shift. Each experiment below gives its key setup. Full details are in App. B.

4.2 Text-to-Video Generation

Setup. We finetune Wan2.1-T2V-14B [85] into a frame-wise pixel-space model at 480×832480\times 832 for 2020K iterations, on 6464K videos generated by Wan2.1. We use shift s=11s=11, which gives the DiT nearly the same effective shift as the best 1.3B setting (Sec. 4.6). We evaluate on VBench [39] with its 946946 GPT-enhanced prompts and five videos per prompt, and run a pairwise human study on 100100 random prompts from Movie Gen Video Bench [69] comparing visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment. We compare against our base latent model, Wan2.1-T2V-14B, and the concurrent pixel-space model PixelUMM [88] using their official settings (App. B.2). Since our models generate 2121 frames, we score every model on the first 1.31.3 s of each video, which has no meaningful impact compared to scoring full videos in Tab. 6.

Results. In Tab. 1, PixVid reaches a VBench total of 84.7884.78, above both Wan2.1 (84.0584.05) and PixelUMM (83.7283.72). Replacing the VAE decoder with the detailer head does not cost visual quality: imaging quality, aesthetic quality, and dynamic degree improve over Wan2.1, while consistency and smoothness stay within 1.41.4 points. PixVid also achieves the highest semantic score of 82.1582.15; color is the only semantic dimension where it trails Wan2.1 by more than a point (81.5981.59 vs. 84.7384.73). In the human study in Fig. 4, raters prefer PixVid across all comparisons, showing that finetuning is competitive with the pretrained latent model and compares favorably with PixelUMM, which is trained from scratch.

4.3 Efficient High-Resolution Generation

Setup. We generate 960×1664960\times 1664 videos with the same 30×5230\times 52 token grid per frame as 480×832480\times 832 generation by doubling the patch size from 1616 to 3232. We first train a patch-16 pixel model at 480×832480\times 832, then finetune it at 960×1664960\times 1664 with patch 3232 with twice the shift and an additional scale-22 calibration. We train on 4040K synthetic videos resized and cropped to the training resolution, and evaluate with the same VBench protocol as Sec. 4.2.

Results. Using the same number of tokens per frame as 480480p, the 960×1664960\times 1664 model reaches the highest VBench total of 85.0985.09 and the best imaging, aesthetic, background-consistency, and temporal-flickering scores in Tab. 1. Its semantic score of 80.6880.68 is below the 480×832480\times 832 model’s, mostly in color. Doubling the patch size therefore keeps PixVid competitive at 44 times the pixels per frame. Its cost per clip stays close to a latent model’s at this resolution: a 2121-frame clip has 32,76032,760 tokens and takes 192192 s on one B200, against 37,44037,440 tokens and 176176 s for a Wan2.1-VAE latent model (App. B.7). Since VBench resizes frames to at most 512512 pixels before scoring, it does not measure the added detail, which we show in Fig. 1(a).

4.4 Precise Video Editing

Setup. We add the control branch of VACE [43] to PixVid-1.3B and finetune it to re-render a video from its per-frame depth and a caption. We compare with VACE-1.3B, finetuned with the same control branch, data, and training settings; and with off-the-shelf depth-conditioned models without finetuning. We train on 7979K stock videos with varied camera and object motion and paired depth [16], and evaluate on 1,0001{,}000 held-out clips across alignment, temporal fidelity, and video quality. Alignment is measured by optical flow error, the fraction of source motion kept, and depth error, while temporal fidelity and video quality are measured by temporal LPIPS, FVMD [54], and FVD [82]. Fast clips are the quarter with the most motion; details are in App. B.4.

Results. PixVid keeps the scene intact under fast motion, where the latent model morphs and blurs moving objects (Fig. 5). On fast clips, it lowers motion error by 40%40\% and depth error by 20%20\%, and keeps 98%98\% of the source motion, against 83%83\% for the finetuned latent model and at most 63%63\% for the zero-shot models (Tab. 2). It also has the lowest FVMD and tLP and leads on all four per-clip metrics over all 1,0001{,}000 clips (Tab. 7), while its FVD trails (118118 vs. 9191).

4.5 Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation

Setup. We lift the bidirectional SolarWM-5B base [37] into pixel space and distill it with Self Forcing [38] into a 44-step causal student that generates one frame per block. We compare with the official causal student distilled from the same base, referred to as SolarWM, which generates blocks of 1212 frames (33 latents). We evaluate quality and camera following on camera paths from nine public datasets, and responsiveness on abrupt turns, measuring how closely the generated motion follows each control (App. B.5). We measure control-to-screen latency, which includes both the wait for controls from the same block and the model’s generation time. We time both models on one B200 GPU with the same kernels.

Results. PixVid cuts median control-to-screen latency from 495495 ms to 3434 ms (Tab. 3). Most of SolarWM’s latency is waiting for controls from the same 1212-frame block, so at 1616 fps a control waits up to 688688 ms before generation even begins. A one-latent block would still wait 33 frames, and our experiments find finetuning SolarWM to one-latent blocks hurts performance (App. B.5). Frame-wise generation lowers throughput, since every frame has its own tokens: PixVid needs about 3×3\times SolarWM’s DiT FLOPs per frame and runs at 29.429.4 vs. 72.072.0 fps, but both models exceed their base Wan model’s native 1616 fps, so both stream in real time. SolarWM’s extra throughput cannot shorten its control-to-screen latency.

PixVid follows abrupt turns more closely (Turn 0.950.95 vs. 0.700.70; Fig. 7), since it receives a camera pose for every frame, whereas SolarWM receives one per four-frame latent. Its FVD is comparable to SolarWM’s (51.151.1 vs. 53.853.8), while its camera rotation and translation errors are higher (5.44∘5.44^{\circ} vs. 4.24∘4.24^{\circ} and 0.3120.312 vs. 0.2310.231). This is likely due to drift accumulated over a longer sequence of poses. Indeed, at 2121 frames our errors are comparable to SolarWM’s (Tab. 9). Mitigating such drift is an active area of research, so we leave it to future work.

4.6 Ablation Study

Setup. All ablations finetune Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for 1010K iterations and change one design choice at a time from our final recipe: the convolutional head, 𝒙\bm{x}-prediction, and shift. We generate one video for each of 119119 VBench prompts and measure the artifact that each choice targets using three reference-free metrics defined in App. B.6: Seam, discontinuities along the patch grid; Noise, the per-pixel noise level; and Flicker, noise that changes from frame to frame. The noise shift decides how training and sampling are spread across noise levels, which affects global structure as well as local noise, so we score the shift sweep on VBench, with all 946946 prompts and one video per prompt.

Results. Output head. A linear head maps each DiT token to its pixel patch independently, so the head itself does not make neighboring patches agree at their borders, and the patch grid stays visible (Fig. 8). Our convolutional head, whose kernels span patch borders, lowers the seam measure from 118.6118.6 to 13.313.3. The U-Net head, which additionally encodes the noisy input, reaches a similar seam (9.29.2) with slightly higher noise (0.8480.848 vs. 0.7770.777) and flicker (0.4290.429 vs. 0.4060.406), and it has 5.6×5.6\times more parameters (248248M vs. 4444M at 1.31.3B), so we use the decoder-only head.

Prediction target. As shown in Fig. 9, 𝒗\bm{v}-prediction with our head fills the video with flickering high-frequency noise at 8080 times the noise level of 𝒙\bm{x}-prediction, because predicting velocity requires the network to reproduce the per-pixel noise of its input. Asymmetric 𝒗\bm{v}-prediction [13] reduces the seams of the linear head (24.524.5 vs. 118.6118.6), but its linear recovery rule still leaves nearly twice the seams of our head, and the noisy input it reads raises noise and flicker (0.8970.897 and 0.5240.524) above those of 𝒙\bm{x}-prediction.

Noise shift. Since pixels are more redundant than latents, the SNR-aligned timestep calibration in App. A.1 naturally dictates a higher shift for pixel models. Here we ablate the uncalibrated shift ss.

Table 4 shows that VBench peaks at s=15s=15 in both total and semantic score, with s=5s=5 close behind in total (84.2784.27 vs. 84.4084.40), and declines at larger shifts, mostly in spatial relationship and multiple objects. We therefore use s=15s=15, giving an effective shift of 3.973.97 under scale c=3.78c=3.78. For the other models we keep a similar effective shift: s=11s=11 for the 14B model gives an effective shift of 3.863.86 under c=2.85c=2.85, and at 960×1664960\times 1664 we double both the shift and the calibration.

Sampler. Latent video models, including Wan2.1, typically sample with UniPC [101], which works well with a bf16 sampler state in latent space. In pixel space, a bf16 state makes UniPC drain color, keeping only 91%91\% of the fp32 chroma, whereas Euler keeps it without needing an fp32 state (Fig. 10). We suspect pixel space colors are more sensitive to higher order samplers. We therefore use the Euler sampler and leave further analysis to future work.

5 Conclusion

Latent video diffusion models compress video in space and time with a VAE. PixVid removes this compression by efficiently finetuning a pretrained latent model to generate every frame directly in pixels, reaching quality competitive with the original model. Working frame by frame in pixels, it overcomes three structural limitations of latent models: resolution scaling, control alignment under fast motion, and control-to-screen latency.

Limitations and future work. Without temporal compression, PixVid processes 3.9×3.9\times as many tokens per second of video as Wan2.1 at 480×832480\times 832, so short low-resolution clips cost more than with a latent model, although the gap closes at higher resolution and streaming stays faster than real time (App. B.7). Generating directly in pixels also opens up training options that a frozen VAE rules out. Losses and rewards can be defined on pixels, enabling adversarial training and RL with pixel-space rewards. Because all models then share the same output space, distillation across architectures or from mixed teachers also becomes possible.

Appendix A Architecture Details

In this section, we show the model architecture details.

A.1 Input Patch Embedding Initialization

The pretrained DiT reads latent tokens through a linear patch embedding 𝑾\bm{W}, while PixVid reads pixel patches. Following AsymFlow [13], we bridge the two with a linear lift between latent tokens and pixel patches, compose it with 𝑾\bm{W} to initialize the pixel patch embedding, and calibrate the timestep so that the DiT initially receives inputs on the latent trajectory it was trained on.

Pixel-Latent Alignment.

Let 𝒙∈ℝ3​p2\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3p^{2}} be a 1×p×p1\times p\times p pixel patch in normalized OKLab, and 𝒛∈ℝd\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the latent token at the same location, i.e., the VAE latent patchified by the DiT. For Wan2.1 [85], the 8×8\times spatial VAE downsampling and the 1×2×21\times 2\times 2 DiT patch give p=16p=16, so 3​p2=7683p^{2}=768 and d=64d=64. We approximate the VAE encoder by a linear lift 𝒙≈c​𝑨​𝒛\bm{x}\approx c\,\bm{A}\bm{z}, where 𝑨∈ℝ3​p2×d\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{3p^{2}\times d} has orthonormal columns (𝑨⊤​𝑨=𝑰d\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A}=\bm{I}_{d}) and c>0c>0 is a scalar. Collecting NN paired patches and tokens from 500500 training clips into 𝑿∈ℝ3​p2×N\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{3p^{2}\times N} and 𝒁∈ℝd×N\bm{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, we fit 𝑨\bm{A} by orthogonal Procrustes [75],

𝑨=arg​min𝐀⊤​𝐀=𝐈d⁡‖𝐗−𝐀𝐙‖F2=𝐔𝐕⊤,\bm{A}=\argmin_{\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A}=\bm{I}_{d}}\|\bm{X}-\bm{A}\bm{Z}\|_{F}^{2}=\bm{U}\bm{V}^{\top}, (4)

where 𝑿​𝒁⊤=𝑼​𝚺​𝑽⊤\bm{X}\bm{Z}^{\top}=\bm{U}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top} is the compact SVD. Procrustes matches directions but not magnitudes, so we set the scale by matching Frobenius norms,

c=‖𝑨⊤​𝑿‖F/‖𝒁‖F,c=\|\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{X}\|_{F}\,/\,\|\bm{Z}\|_{F}, (5)

which gives c=2.85c=2.85 for Wan2.1-T2V-14B and c=3.78c=3.78 for Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B.

Patch Embedding.

Since 𝒛≈𝑨⊤​𝒙/c\bm{z}\approx\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{x}/c, we initialize the pixel patch embedding as 𝑾​𝑨⊤\bm{W}\bm{A}^{\top}, with the bias copied from the pretrained embedding. The 1/c1/c factor is absorbed into the input calibration below. Components of 𝒙\bm{x} outside the span of 𝑨\bm{A} are initially discarded, and the patch embedding is trained with the rest of the model to pick them up.

Internal Timestep Calibration.

Projecting a noisy pixel patch 𝒙σ=(1−σ)​𝒙+σ​ϵ\bm{x}_{\sigma}=(1-\sigma)\,\bm{x}+\sigma\,\bm{\epsilon} onto the lift gives

𝑨⊤​𝒙σ≈c⁡(1−σ)​𝒛+σ​ϵz,\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\sigma}\approx c(1-\sigma)\,\bm{z}+\sigma\,\bm{\epsilon}_{z}, (6)

where ϵz=𝑨⊤​ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d)\bm{\epsilon}_{z}=\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}_{d}) stays standard Gaussian since 𝑨\bm{A} has orthonormal columns. Its signal-to-noise ratio is that of the latent flow at the noise level σ′\sigma^{\prime} satisfying (1−σ′)/σ′=c⁡(1−σ)/σ(1-\sigma^{\prime})/\sigma^{\prime}=c(1-\sigma)/\sigma, i.e.,

σ′=σc⁡(1−σ)+σ.\sigma^{\prime}=\frac{\sigma}{c(1-\sigma)+\sigma}. (7)

Rescaling the input by k⁡(σ)=σ′/σ=1/(c⁡(1−σ)+σ)k(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime}/\sigma=1/\big(c(1-\sigma)+\sigma\big) further matches the magnitude,

k⁡(σ)​𝑨⊤​𝒙σ≈(1−σ′)​𝒛+σ′​ϵz,k(\sigma)\,\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\sigma}\approx(1-\sigma^{\prime})\,\bm{z}+\sigma^{\prime}\,\bm{\epsilon}_{z}, (8)

which is a sample of the pretrained latent flow at noise level σ′\sigma^{\prime}. We therefore feed the DiT the input k⁡(σ)​𝒙σk(\sigma)\,\bm{x}_{\sigma} with timestep σ′\sigma^{\prime} throughout training and sampling. Since c>1c>1, σ′<σ\sigma^{\prime}<\sigma: at the same σ\sigma, the redundant pixels carry more signal than the latents, and the calibration accounts for it by shifting the noise schedule seen by the DiT, as ablated in Sec. 4.6. Unlike AsymFlow, which predicts velocity and inherits the pretrained output head through a calibrated output conversion, PixVid predicts 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}} with a newly initialized detailer, so no output calibration is needed.

A.2 Detailer Head

The detailer head replaces the linear output head and the VAE decoder of the pretrained latent model, mapping DiT features directly to pixels (Fig. 11). Its input is the last DiT hidden state 𝒔\bm{s} on the token grid of size H/p×W/pH/p\times W/p with width DD. We add the timestep embedding 𝒆t\bm{e}_{t} to 𝒔\bm{s}, apply a SiLU, and project the result with a 3×1×13\times 1\times 1 bottleneck convolution. A stack of Up Blocks then upsamples the features to the full resolution H×WH\times W, and a final 3×1×13\times 1\times 1 convolution outputs the pixel prediction 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}}. Since the head upsamples only spatially, it keeps the temporal resolution of the token grid. Each Up Block doubles the spatial resolution, so a 1×16×161\times 16\times 16 patch requires 44 Up Blocks, with widths C4,…,C1C_{4},\dots,C_{1}. We use D=1536D=1536 and C=[512,256,128,64]C=[512,256,128,64] for the 1.3B model, and D=5120D=5120 and C=[1024,256,64,64]C=[1024,256,64,64] for the 14B model, giving detailer heads with 4444M and 337337M parameters, respectively.

Up Block.

Each Up Block applies a 1×2×21\times 2\times 2 transposed convolution to double the height and width, followed by a 3×3×33\times 3\times 3 causal convolution and a SiLU. The transposed convolution upsamples each frame independently, and the causal convolution mixes information spatially and across neighboring frames at the new resolution.

Causal Decoding.

All temporal kernels in the head have size 33 and are padded only on the past side, so at every layer output frame tt depends only on input frames t−2t-2, t−1t-1, and tt (Fig. 11, bottom right). Therefore, the head never reads future frames and is compatible with causal, frame-by-frame generation. When decoding a stream, each convolution caches its two most recent input frames, so every new frame is decoded at a constant cost without recomputing earlier frames.

A.3 Detailer Head for Higher Resolution

To generate 960×1664960\times 1664 videos, we double the patch size from 1×p×p1\times p\times p to 1×2​p×2​p1\times 2p\times 2p, so the token grid stays at 30×5230\times 52 per frame while the resolution doubles. Table 5 compares the two detailer heads.

Patch Embedding.

The 1×2​p×2​p1\times 2p\times 2p patch embedding is built from the pretrained 1×p×p1\times p\times p one by repeating each weight over a 2×22\times 2 block and scaling by 14\frac{1}{4}. This is exactly a 2×22\times 2 average pooling 𝒫\mathcal{P} followed by the pretrained patch embedding, so at initialization the DiT sees a 480480p-equivalent input.

Timestep Calibration.

Pooling keeps the signal but halves the standard deviation of the i.i.d. noise, so 2​𝒫​(𝒙σ)​=𝑑​2​(1−σ)​𝒫​(𝒙)+σ​ϵ2\,\mathcal{P}(\bm{x}_{\sigma})\overset{d}{=}2(1-\sigma)\,\mathcal{P}(\bm{x})+\sigma\,\bm{\epsilon}. This has the form of Eq. (6) with c=2c=2, so we apply the calibration of App. A.1 with scale 22, i.e., timestep σ/(2−σ)\sigma/(2-\sigma) and input 22−σ​𝒫​(𝒙σ)\frac{2}{2-\sigma}\,\mathcal{P}(\bm{x}_{\sigma}), on top of the calibration of the patch-pp model. Composing two calibrations multiplies their scales, so the DiT sees a single calibration of Eq. (7) with scale 2​c2c. We also double the noise shift, which keeps the effective shift s/cs/c unchanged, so the DiT sees the same noise schedule as the patch-pp model.

Appendix B Experiment Details

B.1 Common Settings

Videos are represented in the OKLab color space [66], with each channel normalized by its mean and standard deviation over the training data. Unless otherwise noted, models are trained with a global batch size of 6464 on 6464 NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

We use AdamW [56] with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, and no weight decay, with a constant learning rate of 10−510^{-5} for pretrained or warm-initialized modules and 10−410^{-4} for randomly initialized ones, without warmup. Training uses bfloat16, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights with decay 0.9990.999. We set σmin=0.05\sigma_{\min}=0.05, δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}, and λtemp=λLPIPS=0.2\lambda_{\text{temp}}=\lambda_{\text{LPIPS}}=0.2. Both auxiliary losses are computed in sRGB on a random 256×256256\times 256 crop, with LPIPS using a VGG backbone on 44 random frames, and are weighted by ω⁡(σ)/max⁡(σ,σmin)2\omega(\sigma)/\max(\sigma,\sigma_{\min})^{2} with ω⁡(σ)=(1−σ)2/((1−σ)2+κ2​σ2)\omega(\sigma)=(1-\sigma)^{2}/\big((1-\sigma)^{2}+\kappa^{2}\sigma^{2}\big) and κ=0.3\kappa=0.3. We drop the text prompt with probability 0.10.1. At inference, we clamp the guided 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}} to the valid sRGB gamut at every step, and for text-to-video generation use classifier-free guidance [28] of scale 4.04.0 with the default negative prompt of Wan2.1 [85]. We do not clamp in precise video editing (App. B.4), finding this produces more consistent colors.

B.2 Text-to-Video Generation

We train on 6464K landscape videos generated by Wan2.1 at 720×1280720\times 1280, each with 8181 frames at 1616 fps and paired with its generation prompt, sampling random 2121-frame windows resized and cropped to 480×832480\times 832. Training takes about 5757 hours, and the model totals 14.614.6B parameters (App. A.2).

At evaluation, Wan2.1-T2V-14B generates 8181 frames at 1616 fps with its official settings (5050 UniPC steps, guidance 5.05.0, shift 55). PixelUMM generates 9696 frames at 2424 fps with its released settings (3535 UniPC steps, guidance 6.06.0, shift 1010). Our models generate 2121 frames at 1616 fps (480×832480\times 832 or 960×1664960\times 1664) with 5050 Euler steps, guidance 4.04.0, and their training shifts (1111 and 2222). Table 1 scores the first 1.31.3 s of every baseline video, first 2121 frames for Wan2.1 and first 3131 frames for PixelUMM. Table 6 repeats Tab. 1 with the baselines also scored over their full videos, 8181 frames for Wan2.1 and 9696 frames for PixelUMM. Their total scores change by at most 0.100.10 (84.0784.07 and 83.8283.82), so scoring the first 1.31.3 s does not favor PixVid.

Human evaluation.

We sample 100100 random prompts from Movie Gen Video Bench [69] and generate one video per model per prompt, showing raters 2121-frame, 1.31.3 s segments. Each pair is shown side by side in random left/right order without model names, and raters choose the better video, or a tie, for three questions: “Visual quality: Which video looks better in terms of sharpness, detail, and absence of artifacts?”, “Motion quality: Which video has more natural and smooth motion, without flickering or objects deforming?”, and “Text alignment: Which video better matches the text prompt?”. 1010 raters provided 100100 votes each per comparison.

B.3 Efficient High-Resolution Generation

Starting from Wan2.1-T2V-14B, we first train a patch-16 pixel model at 480×832480\times 832 for 99K iterations (shift 1111, 2828 hours), and then finetune it at 960×1664960\times 1664 with patch 3232 for 2020K iterations (shift 2222, 7373 hours). The 39.839.8K training videos are generated using the captions of our text-to-video data as prompts; we sample random 2121-frame windows at 2424 fps, cropped and downsampled to the training resolution.

B.4 Precise Video Editing

Data and Training.

The training data are 7979K stock videos (74%74\% ground-level, 26%26\% aerial) with captions and Video Depth Anything [16] depth, as 2121-frame windows at 1616 fps and 480×832480\times 832. The latent baseline, VACE-1.3B [43], passes both video and depth through the Wan2.1 VAE. For PixVid, we convert Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B to pixel space (2020K iterations) and add VACE’s control branch, without the LPIPS loss. Both models are finetuned for 1010K iterations, taking about 88 hours for PixVid and 55 for the latent model, and are sampled with the same caption and seed per clip. Per 2121-frame clip, PixVid’s DiT processes 32,76032{,}760 tokens per pass against the latent model’s 9,3609{,}360, or 7.0×7.0\times the FLOPs (28.328.3 vs. 4.14.1 PFLOPs over 100100 passes, excluding the control branch). The zero-shot Wan2.1-Fun-1.3B-Control and Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control models use ZoeDepth input maps, and Cosmos-Transfer2.5 completed 962962 of the 1,0001{,}000 clips.

Setup Details.

PixVid uses patch size 1616 and a four-level detailer; depth enters only through the control tokens. Both models are trained with shift 55 and a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, or 10−410^{-4} for PixVid’s newly initialized control parameters. PixVid samples with 5050 Euler steps and the latent model with Wan’s default 5050-step UniPC, both at shift 55. On 6060 separate clips, we select the guidance scale (and, for PixVid, whether to clamp) by choosing the setting whose static-region sharpness is closest to the source among those within 3%3\% of the lowest flow error. This yields a scale of 33 for the latent model and a scale of 2.52.5 without the clamp for PixVid.

Evaluation.

The 1,0001{,}000 test clips come from 1,0001{,}000 held-out videos. We split them into four bins of 250250 clips each based on the 9595th percentile of source optical flow, namely slow (<10.1<10.1 px/frame), moderate (10.110.1–29.529.5), medium (29.529.5–64.664.6), and fast (≥64.6\geq 64.6). Flow is estimated with NeuFlow v2 [100]. Motion error is the end-point error between the flows of the generated and source videos, and motion kept is the ratio of their 9595th-percentile flow magnitudes. Depth error is the AbsRel between Video Depth Anything estimates on the generated and source videos, aligned per clip in scale and shift. Temporal LPIPS compares the perceptual change between consecutive frames of the generated and source videos. We report medians over clips, with per-bin results in Tab. 7, except for FVD and FVMD, which are set-level. FVMD uses the 962962 clips completed by all models, and FVD uses all clips each model completed. PixVid has lower motion error than the finetuned latent model on 88%88\% of fast motion clips (84%84\% over all clips).

Error Analysis.

On fast clips, the latent model’s motion errors spike every four frames, at transitions between latents. A VAE round trip of the source video has a motion error of 2.02.0 px on these clips and adds only 0.070.07 px at latent transitions, against 1.651.65 px for the latent model, so the errors arise in generation rather than in the VAE.

B.5 Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation

Setup.

Both 44-step students stream 8181 frames at 480×864480\times 864 and 1616 fps from a first frame, a caption, and a camera path. SolarWM is the official SolarWM-5B student [37], which uses the Wan2.2 VAE with 4×4\times temporal compression. For PixVid, we lift the bidirectional base with patch size 3232, matching its VAE’s 16×16\times spatial compression and 2×22\times 2 DiT patch, and distill it with Self Forcing [38] for 33K iterations with a noisy KV cache, keeping the 44 sink frames clean. Both students are compared with EMA weights. As references, we also evaluate the bidirectional latent base at 5050 steps and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [85] without camera input.

Evaluation.

The 807807 camera paths come from nine sources: ABot-World [42], MultiCamVideo [3], DL3DV [52], Sekai walking and game [51], RealCam-Vid [102], SpatialVID [86], MiraData [44], and OmniWorld [103]; SolarWM’s camera-translation filter removed 9393 of 900900 planned clips. FID uses 2020 frames per clip and FVD [82] 55 windows of 1616 frames. We also report the six VBench [39] dimensions that apply to arbitrary videos: subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, and imaging quality (Tab. 8). Camera following uses poses estimated by ViPE [36], reporting rotation error, translation error, CamMC, and frame-to-frame rotation error.

Responsiveness.

The 100100 abrupt-turn paths (5050 from RealCam-Vid, 5050 from DL3DV) are rotation-only and have no ground-truth video: each is a random sequence of holds, yaw turns and pitch turns at 1.51.5–2.5∘2.5^{\circ} per frame, mixing 88–1414-frame moves with 22–55-frame jerks. We estimate the horizontal image shift between consecutive frames by phase correlation; Turn in Tab. 3 is its correlation with the yaw control per frame, pooled over all clips, and PixVid’s per-clip correlation is higher on every clip. Each model receives the whole path up front, so this measures how closely the motion follows the controls, not latency. SolarWM receives the camera pose once per four-frame latent, at frames 0,1,5,…,770,1,5,\dots,77, so it cannot place a turn within a latent and spreads brief turns over neighboring frames, resulting in lower Turn of 0.700.70 compared to PixVid at 0.950.95.

Rollout Length.

In Tab. 9, we evaluate the same generations over the first 2121, 4141, and all 8181 frames. PixVid’s rotation error is slightly worse than SolarWM’s over the first 2121 and 4141 frames, and its translation error is moderately higher, but the gap in camera following grows with the rollout length. In terms of visual quality, PixVid achieves lower FVD at every rollout length.

Timing.

We time both students on one B200 at 480×864480\times 864 with 44 denoising steps, after the local attention window has filled, on our custom inference stack built with optimized CuTeDSL kernels. A SolarWM latent covers 44 pixel frames totalling 405405 tokens, while PixVid uses 405405 tokens for every frame, so SolarWM has higher throughput (72.072.0 vs. 29.429.4 fps). For an isolated control, the control for frame tt arrives at t/16t/16 s and a block starts once its last control has arrived, so SolarWM’s latency is its wait (00–688688 ms) plus its block compute time (151151 ms), giving 151151–839839 ms (median 495495 ms), against 3434 ms for PixVid. SolarWM’s official implementation, with its streaming VAE decoder, is slower: it takes 543543 ms in the DiT and 205205 ms in the VAE per 1212-frame block (16.116.1 fps), for a median latency of 1,0911{,}091 ms (Tab. 10). Per generated frame, PixVid’s DiT needs 3.0×3.0\times SolarWM’s FLOPs (16.416.4 vs. 5.65.6 TFLOPs), and its throughput is 2.4×2.4\times lower.

One-Latent SolarWM.

The official SolarWM student generates 33-latent (1212-frame) blocks, waiting up to 1111 frames for controls. Since a latent model’s minimum block is one latent (44 frames), we test whether shrinking SolarWM to one-latent blocks narrows the responsiveness gap to PixVid. We train a 44-step, one-latent SolarWM-5B student on the same clean-81f data  [37] over a 1515-latent history window following SolarWM’s official recipe, finetuning the teacher-forced AnyFlow Stage 1 checkpoint with one-latent blocks until convergence (44K iterations), followed by Stage 2 DMD distillation (400400 iterations).

Figure 12 shows One-latent SolarWM produces lower-quality camera following and output. This is reflected in Tab. 11, which also shows latency of the one-latent model is still higher than PixVid.

B.6 Ablations

All ablations use Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with calibration scale c=3.78c=3.78; the shift sweep uses the decoder-only head and 𝒙\bm{x}-prediction, and the head and prediction ablations use s=15s=15. VBench in Tab. 4 uses all 946946 prompts with one video each, sampled and scored as in Sec. 4.2. The 119119 prompts are every eighth of VBench’s 946946, sampled with 5050 Euler steps in bfloat16. All metrics are computed on grayscale frames. Noise estimates the per-pixel noise standard deviation in 8-bit levels [40]. Flicker applies the same estimator to the temporal residual, the video minus its temporal Gaussian blur (σ=1.2\sigma=1.2 frames). Seam measures discontinuities on the 16×1616\times 16 patch grid. For each pixel column, we take the mean squared brightness difference to the next column over all rows and frames; at each patch border, we subtract the median of the six neighboring columns and take the median over borders, averaging the horizontal and vertical directions. Noise that is independent across pixels adds the same amount at every column and cancels; we subtract the same quantity measured 44 pixels from the patch borders, where no seam occurs, and report the result in squared 8-bit levels.

B.7 Compute Cost

Table 12 gives the cost of text-to-video inference. FLOPs count the matrix multiplications of the DiT and the detailer head, including attention; we time each component with random weights on one B200, taking the median of 1010 runs after 33 warmup runs. Without temporal compression, a 2121-frame 480×832480\times 832 clip has 3.5×3.5\times as many tokens as Wan2.1’s latents (32,76032{,}760 vs. 9,3609{,}360) and, since attention grows quadratically with the token count, 5.8×5.8\times the FLOPs. Figure 13 shows doubling the resolution reverses this: a latent model’s tokens grow 4×4\times and its FLOPs 6.9×6.9\times, while PixVid keeps 30×5230\times 52 tokens per frame, so only its detailer grows and its FLOPs rise by 17%, matching the latent model at 960×1664960\times 1664. At that resolution, PixVid still takes 9% longer (192 vs. 176 s), because its detailer runs convolutions on full-resolution frames, which use the GPU less efficiently than the DiT’s matrix multiplications.

Appendix C Qualitative Results

To demonstrate the advantages of our approach, we show additional qualitative comparisons.

C.1 Text-to-Video Generation

In Fig. 14, we show additional qualitative comparisons between PixVid, Wan2.1-T2V-14B and PixelUMM. PixVid produces high-quality videos, often with the most detail. PixelUMM struggles with more flicker and artifacts.

C.2 High-Resolution Generation

Initialized from Wan2.1-T2V-14B, which generates 8181-frame videos at 480×832480\times 832, and trained as described in App. B.3, PixVid spends the same token budget on resolution instead of duration: our method generates 2121-frame videos at 960×1664960\times 1664 with much finer pixel-level details because it directly generates pixels without any VAEs that compress and reconstruct them, as shown in Fig. 15. We show the 10th frame of each generated video, and the full videos are on our project page.

C.3 Precise Video Editing

To evaluate how well our method handles sharp motion compared to latent-space approaches, we show additional depth-to-video results in Fig. 16. We compare PixVid-1.3B against Cosmos-Transfer2.5-2B [64], Wan2.1-Fun-1.3B-Control [1], VACE-1.3B [43], and VACE-1.3B finetuned with the same data and settings as ours. We show one frame per clip from fast-motion clips; quantitative results over all 1,0001{,}000 held-out clips are in Tab. 7. Under such fast motion, the baselines, all of which compress several frames into each latent, often lose scene structure or blur, while our pixel-space model follows the depth more closely.

C.4 Camera-Controlled Autoregressive Generation

In Fig. 17, we show additional qualitative comparisons between SolarWM-5B and PixVid-5B under camera-controlled autoregressive generation. Both models use the same Wan 2.2 5B backbone and receive the same camera controls. PixVid-5B reaches a lower FVD (Tab. 3), although its imaging and aesthetic scores are lower (Tab. 8). PixVid-5B accumulates drift during autoregressive generation, which leads to slightly larger rotation and translation errors. We leave this to future work.
